newsitem.title: USA: Billionaire Allen central to Seattle stadium vote.
newsitem.headline: Billionaire Allen central to Seattle stadium vote.

text.p: Washington state voters will decide the fate of a proposed $425 million Seattle football stadium on Tuesday in a contest that pits poorly funded opponents against the vast resources of billionaire Paul Allen.

Voters are well aware that Allen, worth more than $13 billion as co-founder of Microsoft Corp., could write a check for the proposed 72,000-seat open-air stadium to house the Seattle Seahawks, which he wants to buy.

But a carefully constructed tax package and massive television advertising campaign appear to have given the proposal at least an even chance of passing in the special election, according to recent opinion polls.
"The momentum pretty clearly looks to be on the proponents' side," said local political analyst Stuart Elway. "Whether it overcomes the initial opposition remains to be seen."

Allen, who counts the Portland Trail Blazers basketball team among his many holdings, emerged as a white knight in April 1996, when he bought an option on the Seahawks to keep the team from being moved out of town.

But he has insisted he will walk away from the deal without a new stadium to provide public funds to replace the 21-year-old Kingdome, which most residents agree is a concrete blot on the downtown skyline.

"If you say no, that means no for me too, because I'm not going to do this without you," the famously shy entrepreneur says in a television ad which has marked his only public statement of the whirlwind six-week campaign.
Allen has contributed nearly $5 million to the pro-stadium campaign, allowing one of the most expensive television advertising blitzes in state history.
At the request of state political leaders he has taken the unprecedented step of funding the entire $4 million cost of the statewide election.

Bert Kolde, vice chairman of Allen's Football Northwest, said Washington state voters must decide between the "two futures" of an inadequate Kingdome or a state-of-the-art football, soccer and exhibition facility.
"The Kingdome will suck a quarter of a billion dollars in property taxes over the next 20 years," Kolde said. "The question is, which asset is more valuable to the community?"
Opponents say the money could be better spent on schools, roads and parks.

"It is difficult to paint the true picture because they've done such a good job of hiding how this takes money from the state Treasury," said state Rep. Tim Sheldon. "You're going to have less available for nursing home care, there's going to be less available for schools."

Opponents have been able to raise only about $200,000 for a few cable television ads, although they got a boost Thursday when consumer activist Ralph Nader held a fund-raising luncheon in Seattle and denounced the stadium proposal as "the cutting edge of corporate welfare greed."

The stadium package, approved narrowly by the Legislature after a rancorous battle, includes $101 million from existing sales taxes, $127 million from lottery games, $56 million in stadium admissions and parking taxes and $40 million in hotel room taxes.
Allen has agreed to contribute $50 million of his own money and $50 million from the sale of seat licenses as well as cover any cost overruns.

Stadium elections have become an increasingly common feature of the U.S. political landscape, and even Kolde acknowledged that Allen's group faced an "environment of resentment" toward professional sports when the campaign began.
"I think this vote will probably go down to the wire," he said, noting that San Francisco voters last week approved a football stadium issue by less than one percent of votes cast.
"People are clearly fed up with pro sports as an institution," said Elway, the political analyst. "But when it comes right down to it, people say, 'I don't want to lose our team, so I'll vote yes.'"
